**This document records why things changed. It is not a spec.** The planning docs (00–11) always hold current truth; if they ever disagree with this log, they win.

Kept because the reasoning is the valuable part — and because "here's a project where I made and documented real tradeoffs" is directly useful material for engineering leadership interviews.

Newest first.

---

## 2 Aug 2026 (later) — Meal grouping reversed, recents promoted into MVP

### REVERSED: group the day by meal

**Was:** `meal_type` on `FoodEntry`, defaulted from time of day, with Today and history grouped into breakfast / lunch / dinner / snack. Accepted from external feedback earlier the same day.

**Now:** cut. Entries are a simple reverse-chronological list.

**Why:** the feedback assumed a meal-structured eater. Grazing through the day is equally common, and in that pattern meal buckets are noise — they force a decision every time something doesn't fit one, and moving an entry between meals means re-logging it. The organizing unit that actually matters is the day, which the model already has.

A good reminder that feedback about *how people eat* is feedback about the person giving it.

### Quantity multipliers are in — they were never what ±5 steppers meant

Two things had been conflated under "steppers":

* **±5 calorie nudges** — still cut. Nobody knows whether five is the right increment
* **Quantity multipliers** — in. "I had two of these" is a question people can answer instantly

Stored as `FoodItem.quantity`, with item macros held per single portion and multiplied on read.

### PROMOTED FROM PARKED: recents

**Was:** saved foods / quick add, parked as "highest-value v2."

**Now:** in MVP.

**Why:** the trigger was noticing that eating the same protein bar twice in a day meant two photos, two vision API calls, and two stored images for one known food. Extend that across recurring staples — shakes, packaged items, a fixed breakfast — and most logging is re-photographing things the app already knows.

The cost is small now that line items exist: one endpoint listing distinct prior `FoodItem`s, and a picker that copies values into a new entry. No separate saved-foods model — history *is* the library.

The economics are the real argument. This is the difference between paying for a vision call on every logged food and paying only for genuinely new ones.

### Re-log versus multiply — two distinct actions

Worth recording because the distinction is easy to lose:

* **Multiply** — ate two at once. Adjust `quantity` on the existing item
* **Re-log** — ate one now, another four hours later. New entry, new `eaten_at`, values copied

Doubling an earlier entry to represent a later serving would claim both were eaten at the original time. Re-logging keeps the timeline honest at identical cost.

### Photo becomes an input method, not the organizing principle

Consequence of the above: `FoodEntry.photo_key` and `ai_raw_response` become nullable, and a `source` field records whether an entry came from a photo, from recents, or from manual entry.

The app is a macro log that happens to have an excellent camera-based input. That's a subtly different product from a photo diary, and a better one.

## 2 Aug 2026 — External product feedback review

Five changes accepted, one rejected, one core decision reversed.

### REVERSED: one photo = one entry, no line items

**Was:** one photo produces one entry with total macros, no per-food breakdown. Chosen early for a simpler model and simpler UI.

**Now:** `FoodEntry` holds one or more `FoodItem` children.

**Why:** the constraint had become the wall four separate features ran into — per-item correction, saved foods, meal planning, and recipes. When that many things pile up behind one decision, the decision is usually the mistake.

**What made it safe:** line items in the *model* don't require line items in the *primary UI*. Review still leads with entry totals; items are a secondary list touched only when something's wrong.

**Timing:** had to land before E4 built `FoodEntry`. After production data exists it's a migration, not an edit.

→ Docs 02, 06

### Accepted: Sign in with Apple only

**Was:** email/password with verification and reset, plus Sign in with Apple.

**Now:** Apple only. Three screens deleted.

**Why:** email/password is the worst first impression a mobile app can make, and it dragged in deliverability as a failure mode. It also removed a real trap — a blocking verification email inside an unexitable onboarding stack meant an undelivered email left the user with no path forward.

**Rejected outright:** phone + SMS. Per-message cost, another vendor, and strictly worse than one Face ID tap on iOS. Google OAuth adds little on an iOS-only app.

**Cost accepted:** less Django auth surface to learn — no password hashing, verification tokens, or reset flows. Retained the more interesting half: JWT issuance, rotation, blacklisting, and third-party identity-token verification.

→ Doc 04

### Accepted: six onboarding questions, resequenced after the first meal

**Was:** ten questions before anything else.

**Now:** six, and they come after the user has logged and seen their first meal analyzed.

**Why:** demanding effort before demonstrating value is the worst possible activation shape. Six questions cover Mifflin-St Jeor; the other four were refinement and moved to settings.

**Consequence:** `DailyLog.target_version` becomes nullable, backfilled when targets are first created.

→ Docs 02, 05

### Accepted: correction is per-item, steppers stay dead

`±5` buttons were already cut — a user has no idea whether five is the right increment. The feedback independently reached the same conclusion, which was good validation.

Correction is now: adjust an item's portion, correct what an item is, or add/remove an item. Whole-plate scaling remains as a shortcut. Portion scaling is the right mental model — people think "that was half a serving," not "that was 47 fewer calories."

→ Doc 06

### Accepted: description prominent, image metadata gone

The text box was always specified as a strong signal that should override the photo. Its absence from the drawings was a design bug, not a plan gap.

File size, dimensions, and format removed from the UI entirely — engineer-brain leaking into a consumer surface.

→ Doc 06

### Accepted then reversed: group the day by meal

`meal_type` was added to `FoodEntry` on the strength of this feedback, then cut later the same day. See the entry above.

### Accepted in principle, not built: meal planning

The strongest strategic point in the feedback — macro apps are diaries, and the useful version is a *tool*. Finding out at 9pm that you're 60g short is a failure the current design doesn't prevent.

Not in MVP: planning is a second product with its own screens, model, and habits. But the line-item reversal unblocks it, which is exactly why that reversal happened before E4 rather than after.

→ Follow-ups

## 2 Aug 2026 — Design review (doc 21)

### Streaks cut entirely

Originally a core requirement. Removed from MVP — the chip on Today, the screen behind the menu, and the delete-confirmation warning all go.

Side effect: settles the open `DailyLog` deletion edge case. With no streak, whether the row survives its last entry stops mattering.

### No push notifications

Flow 05 opened the recap from a morning notification. Cut.

APNs setup, EAS config, delivery scheduling — and the real cost, a second permission prompt stacked on camera. Permission fatigue is a genuine conversion problem on iOS, and camera is the permission that must succeed.

Replaced by a card on Today. Adding push later costs nothing in redesign.

### Layer 3 gated on habit, not payment

Post-day coaching unlocks after four weeks of logging rather than behind a paywall.

Tradeoff accepted knowingly: once it unlocks permanently, it can't become paid without taking something away from existing users.

### Offline is an epic, not a state

The design listed "offline queue" as a global interrupt state. That was optimistic. MVP requires connectivity to log; capture is blocked with a clear state rather than half-saving.

→ E12 placeholder

### Three macros, not four

The design draft referenced four. The model has three — calories, protein, fiber. Three is the product thesis; carbs and fat are parked.

## Earlier decisions worth remembering

**The day is an entity.** `DailyLog` as a real row rather than a computed local date. Grouping, "log to yesterday", and historical target accuracy all fall out of it. Still the single best structural decision in the project.

**Targets are append-only.** Slowly-changing-dimension pattern. Eliminates the "why did last month's numbers change?" bug class.

**Typed API contract.** drf-spectacular → Orval → React Query hooks, with CI failing on drift. Rename a serializer field and the mobile app fails to compile rather than returning `undefined` in TestFlight.

**Deploy at ticket six, not ticket forty.** Everything after E1 ships to a real environment.

**Hybrid target generation.** Mifflin-St Jeor computed deterministically, passed to the model as a baseline for adjustment and explanation. Arithmetic stays reproducible; the model contributes judgment. The concrete example of when *not* to hand something to an LLM.

**The** `logging` **app naming trap.** An app called `logging` shadows Python's stdlib module and breaks imports. Use `entries`.
